parole.significato: Forms names for real or imaginary dinosaurs.
parole.testo: From translingual and New Latin forms of Ancient Greek σαῦρος (saûros, “lizard, reptile”), used in taxonomic names of various dinosaurs.

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Acer; a maple.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Acer, from Latin acer (“maple tree”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a family of plants, Araceae, of which the genus Arum is the type.
parole.testo: From translingual Arum + -aceous, from Latin arum, a genus of plants, from Ancient Greek ἄρον (áron).

parole.significato: Synonym of spleenwort: any plant of the genus Asplenium.
parole.testo: A genericization of taxonomic name Asplenium (“the spleenworts”), from Linnaeus's New Latin adjustment of Latin asplenon (“spleenwort”), from Ancient Greek ἄσπληνον (ásplēnon, “spleenwort”), from ἀ- (a-, “un-”) + σπλήν (splḗn, “spleen”) + -ον (-on, “-um”), from its use to cure anthrax in livestock.

parole.significato: Any member of the Blattoidea superfamily of cockroaches and termites.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Blattoidea, from the type genus of Blatta, from Latin blatta (“photophobic bug”). Further etymology unclear.

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Bombyx of true silkmoths, whose caterpillars often feed on mulberries.
parole.testo: From translingual Bombyx, from Latin bombyx, from Ancient Greek βόμβυξ (bómbux). Compare bombast.

parole.significato: toad, frog
parole.testo: From translingual Bufo marinus (now Rhinella marina), the cane toad, from Latin būfō (“toad”).

parole.significato: Any member of the family Cactaceae, a family of flowering New World succulent plants suited to a hot, semi-desert clima…
parole.testo: From taxonomic name Cactus, a name given in 1752 by Linnaeus for a genus of cacti (now superseded by the genus name Mammillaria), from Latin cactus, from Ancient Greek κάκτος (káktos, “cardoon”), possibly of Pre-Greek origin.

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Calceolaria.
parole.testo: From translingual Calceolaria, the genus of slipperworts, from Latin calceolus (“slipper, little shoe”) + -āria (“-ary: forming plant names”), from calceus (“calceus, footwear”) + -olus (“-ole: forming diminutives”), , from calx (“heel”) + -eus (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Calendula, with yellow or orange flowers, often called marigolds. Used for decoration, as food o…
parole.testo: From translingual Calendula, New Latin calendula, diminutive of kalendae. See calends.

parole.significato: Any moth in the family Callidulidae.
parole.testo: From translingual Callidulidae, from translingual Callidula + -idae, from Latin callidulus, from callidus + -ulus, from calleō + -idus, from callum (“hard or thick substance, callus”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Campanula.
parole.testo: From translingual Campanula, from Latin campānula, diminutive of campāna (“bell”).

parole.significato: A yeast of the genus Candida, usually specifically Candida albicans
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Candida, from Latin candida.

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Canna of tropical plants with large leaves and often showy flowers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Canna, from Latin canna (“reed”), from Ancient Greek κᾰ́ννᾰ (kắnnă, “reed”), from Akkadian 𒂵𒉡𒌑𒌝 (qanûm). Cognates Biblical Hebrew קָנֶה (qané), Aramaic קַנְיָא (qanyā), Classical Syriac ܩܢܝܐ (qanya), and English canon, cannon, canal, and channel. Doublet of cane and kaneh.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the zoologic infraorder Cetacea, or associated with species falling under that taxonomic hierarchy.
parole.testo: From translingual Cetacea, from Latin cētus (“whale”), + -an.

parole.significato: A green alga of the genus Chara.
parole.testo: From translingual/New Latin Chara.

parole.significato: Any of the genus Cissus of woody vines.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Cissus, from Latin cissus and Ancient Greek κισσός (kissós).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Clematis, vigorous climbing lianas found throughout the temperate zones.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Clematis, from Latin clēmatis, from Ancient Greek κληματίς (klēmatís), from κλῆμα (klêma, “vine, branch with vines”).

parole.significato: Any of several flowers of the genus Colchicum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Colchicum, from Latin colchicum, from Ancient Greek κολχικόν (kolkhikón).

parole.significato: Any of certain plants in the mint family, many used as ornamentals for their colorful, variegated leaves, sometime incl…
parole.testo: From the genus name translingual Coleus, from Latin coleus, from Ancient Greek κολεός (koleós, “sheath”) in reference to the manner in which the stamens are united.

parole.significato: Any snake in the family Colubridae, completely covered in scales and mostly nonvenomous.
parole.testo: From translingual Colubridae, from the genus translingual Coluber, from Latin coluber (“snake”).

parole.significato: Any of a number of tropical trees and shrubs in the genus Combretum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Combretum, from Latin combrētum.

parole.significato: A poisonous glucoside extracted from the lily of the valley (Convallaria majalis)
parole.testo: From translingual Convallaria + Latin amarus (“bitter”).

parole.significato: Any of various mostly Mexican herbs of the genus Cosmos having radiate heads of variously coloured flowers and pinnate…
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Cosmos (genus name), from New Latin cosmos, from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “decoration, ornament; order; universe; the earth, the world”) (referring to its elegant leaves); see further at etymology 1.

parole.significato: Any of several erect or creeping shrubs, of the genus Cotoneaster, that have pinkish flowers and red berries.
parole.testo: From translingual Cotoneaster, from Latin cotōneum (“quince”) + -aster.

parole.significato: Any protozoan of the genus Cryptosporidium, intestinal parasites of humans and other vertebrates that can cause diarrhe…
parole.testo: From translingual Cryptosporidium (the genus name), from Latin crypto- (“hidden”) + sporidium (“spore”). From 20th century.

parole.significato: Any of the genus Curculio of weevils.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Curculio, from Latin curculiō (“weevil”).

parole.significato: Any sedge of genus Cyperus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Cyperus. Further from Latin cypērus and Ancient Greek κύπειρος (kúpeiros).

parole.significato: Any of various tooth shells of the genus Dentalium.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Dentalium, from Latin dentālis (“dental”), dēns (“tooth”), Proto-Italic *dents and Proto-Indo-European *h₃dónts.

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Dentex of perciform fish.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Dentex, from Latin dentex, from Latin dēns (“tooth”). Further from Proto-Italic *dents and Proto-Indo-European *h₃dónts.

parole.significato: A suffrutescent plant of the genus Dictamnus, with strong perfume and showy flowers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Dictamnus, from Latin dictamnum. See dittany.

parole.significato: Any of several plants of the genus Dryas; the mountain avens.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Dryas for the plants, from both Latin Dryas and Ancient Greek Δρῠᾰ́ς (Drŭắs), derived from δρῦς (drûs, “tree, oak”). The second definition comes from the large quantity of pollen from the plant that is found in ice cores dating from these periods.

parole.significato: Any asteraceous flowering plant of the genus Eclipta.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Eclipta, from Latin eclīpta, from Ancient Greek ἐκλείπω (ekleípō, “to leave out, to pass over”).

parole.significato: Any member of the small Emys genus of freshwater pond tortoises.
parole.testo: From the translingual genus name Emys and its etymon, the Classical Latin emys, from the Ancient Greek ἐμύς (emús).

parole.significato: Any in the family Ephemeridae of mayflies.
parole.testo: From translingual Ephemeridae, from New Latin ephemerus, from Ancient Greek ἐφήμερος (ephḗmeros), the more common form of ἐφημέριος (ephēmérios, “of, for, or during the day, living or lasting but for a day, short-lived, temporary”), from ἐπί (epí, “on”) + ἡμέρα (hēméra, “day”).

parole.significato: Calosoma scrutator, a common North American ground beetle which has an iridescent exoskeleton, with large parts on its…
parole.testo: Compound of fiery + searcher. Fiery comes from the orange colors found around the edge of the abdomen. Searcher is a partial calque of translingual Calosoma scrutator, itself from Latin scrūtātor (“searcher, examinator, investigator”), which references its diet of certain other bugs, which it hunts

parole.significato: Any of the parasitic nematode worms of superfamily Filarioidea that lives in the blood of vertebrates and is transmitte…
parole.testo: 19th century, from translingual Filaria (name of type genus), from Latin filum (“thread”).

parole.significato: Any of various fungi, of the genus Fusarium, some of which are pathogenic to plants and animals.
parole.testo: From translingual Fusarium, from Latin fusus (“spindle”).

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Glaucus of nudibranchiate mollusks, found in the warmer latitudes, swimming in the open sea, st…
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Glaucus, from Latin glaucus, from Ancient Greek γλαῦκος (glaûkos, “blue-grey fish”), from γλαυκός (glaukós, “blue-green, blue-grey”).

parole.significato: Any of several passerine birds of the genera Quiscalus, Hypopyrrhus, Lampropsar and Macroagelaius, of the Americas, hav…
parole.testo: From translingual Gracula, from Latin graculus (“jackdaw”).

parole.significato: A rose of the Grandiflora class of roses created in the middle of the 20th century as backcrosses of hybrid teas and fl…
parole.testo: From translingual Grandiflora, from New Latin grandiflōra, the feminine form, following the feminine gender of rosa (“rose”), of grandiflōrus (“having large flowers”), from grandis (“large”) + flōs (“flower”, stem flōr-) + -us (suffix forming adjectives; feminine -a).

parole.significato: A butterfly of the genus Graphium.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Graphium, from Latin graphium (“stylus”). Doublet of graft.

parole.significato: Belonging to the taxonomic subfamily Harpalinae.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Harpalinae. By surface analysis, translingual Harpalus + -ine. Further from Latin Harpalus and Ancient Greek Ἅρπαλος (Hárpalos).

parole.significato: Any of various flowering plants, of the genus Helenium, the dried leaves of which were once used to make a form of snuf…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Translingual Helenium.

parole.significato: Any member of the taxonomic tribe Hominini, the evolutionary group that includes modern humans and now-extinct bipedal…
parole.testo: From translingual Hominini, from the stem of Latin homo (“man”). Compare hominid.

parole.significato: Any of many flowering plants of the genus Hypericum, St. John's worts.
parole.testo: From the genus name, translingual Hypericum, itself from Latin hypericum, from Ancient Greek ὑπερικόν (huperikón), from ὑπέρ (hupér, “over”) + ἐρείκη (ereíkē, “heath”).

parole.significato: Any of various ornamental plants of the genus Impatiens.
parole.testo: From translingual Impatiens, from Latin impatiēns.

parole.significato: Any cruciferous plant of the genus Lepidium, often called garden cresses or pepperworts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Lepidium, from Latin lepidium and Ancient Greek λεπίδιον (lepídion, literally “little scale”), diminutive of λεπίς (lepís, “scale, flake”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Linaria (as the toadflax)
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Linaria, from Latin linarius (“linenary”), from linum (“linen, flax”).

parole.significato: A tree or shrub in any species of the genus Magnolia, many with large flowers and simple leaves.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Magnolia, from French Magnol + -ia. Named after French botanist Pierre Magnol (1638–1715). The surname is a form of the male given name Magne, from Latin magnus, which in turn from Proto-Italic *magnos, from Proto-Indo-European *m̥ǵh₂nós, from *méǵh₂s (“great”). .

parole.significato: A larva, in a stage following the zoea, in the development of most crabs. In this stage the legs and abdominal appendag…
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Megalops and New Latin megalops.

parole.significato: Any fungal infection caused by fungi in the order Mucorales.
parole.testo: From mucor (“mouldy”) + mycosis (“fungal infection”). From translingual Mucorales, from Latin mucor (“mustiness”).

parole.significato: Any infectious bacterium of the genus Mycoplasma, often specifically Mycoplasma pneumoniae
parole.testo: From translingual Mycoplasma, from Latin, from Ancient Greek μύκης (múkēs, “fungus”) + πλάσμα (plásma, “-shaped”). Equivalent to myco- + plasma.

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Nigella of about twelve species of annual flowering plants, the blooms of which are generally bl…
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Nigella, from Late Latin nigella. Doublet of nielle.

parole.significato: Any of the large extinct feliforms of the family Nimravidae, of the Middle to Late Miocene (40—7 million years ago).
parole.testo: From translingual Nimravidae, ultimately from Nimrod + Latin avus (“ancestor”).

parole.significato: Synonym of nodosaurus, Nodosaurus textilis, an ankylosaurian dinosaur of the Cretaceous period lacking a clublike tail.
parole.testo: Clipping of nodosaurus, from translingual Nodosaurus, from New Latin, from Latin nodosus (“knobby, knotted”) + -saurus, equivalent to nodo- + -saur.

parole.significato: Any member of the family †Nodosauridae, ankylosaurians without clublike tails.
parole.testo: From translingual Nodosauridae, from New Latin nodosaurus + -idae, equivalent to nodosaur + -id.

parole.significato: A sea slug belonging to the order Nudibranchia.
parole.testo: Circa 19th century, borrowed from translingual Nudibranchia, from Latin nudus (“naked”) + branchia (“gills”).

parole.significato: A shrub or small tree native to mountains in southwestern North America, Juniperus monosperma
parole.testo: Translated from the taxonomic name: translingual Juniperus is from Latin iuniperus (“juniper”) and monosperma is from Ancient Greek μόνος (mónos, “single, alone”) + σπέρμα (spérma, “seed”)

parole.significato: Any echinoderm of the class Ophiuroidea
parole.testo: From translingual genus name Ophiura (originally species name in Linnaeus), from New Latin ophiurus (“brittle star”), from Ancient Greek ὄφις (óphis, “serpent”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”) (referring to the serpent-like arms of the brittle star). This English form by conflation with suffix -ure (“result o

parole.significato: Opuntia, a genus of cactus that includes such cacti as the prickly pear and xoconostle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Translingual Opuntia.

parole.significato: Any of numerous species of freshwater pectinibranchiate mollusks, sea snails belonging to Viviparus (syn. Paludina), Me…
parole.testo: From translingual Paludina, from Latin palūs (“a marsh, pool”).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Panicum of tropical grasses.
parole.testo: From translingual Panicum (genus name), from New Latin panicum (“panicgrass”).

parole.significato: Any apiaceous plant of the genus Peucedanum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Peucedanum, from Latin peucedanum, from Ancient Greek πευκέδᾰνον (peukédănon), substantivization of Ancient Greek πευκεδᾰνός (peukedănós, “bitter like resin”).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Philadelphus of shrubs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Philadelphus, from Latin Philadelphus, Ancient Greek Φιλάδελφος (Philádelphos), φιλάδελφος (philádelphos).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Picariae, an obsolete bird classification.
parole.testo: From translingual Picariae + -an, from Latin picus (“woodpecker”).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Pisonia of nyctaginaceous flowering plants.
parole.testo: From translingual Pisonia, from New Latin, from the Latin form of Willem Pies, a Dutch doctor and naturalist, + -nia.

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Pittosporum, comprising various Old World shrubs and trees.
parole.testo: A genericization of translingual Pittosporum, from New Latin pittosporum, from Ancient Greek πίττα (pítta, “pitch”) + σπόρος (spóros, “seed, spore”), from the sticky resin surrounding its seeds.

parole.significato: Any of various flatworms of the order Tricladida living in marine, freshwater, or terrestrial environments.
parole.testo: From translingual Planaria (genus) (from Late Latin plānārius (“lying on a plane”), from Latin plānum) + -an.

parole.significato: A low plain.
parole.testo: From translingual planitia, from Latin plānitia.

parole.significato: Any of many shrubs and herbs of the genus Potentilla; the cinquefoils.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Potentilla, from Latin potentilla, from potēns (“strong”) + -illa (dimintuive suffix).

parole.significato: An unstable glucoside found in plants of the buttercup family (Ranunculaceae). On maceration, it is enzymatically broke…
parole.testo: From the intermediary English ranunculus or directly from translingual Ranunculus, from Latin rānunculus (“small frog”) + -in (“chemical compound”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Ranunculus; the buttercup or crowfoot.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Ranunculus, from Latin rānunculus.

parole.significato: of, relating to, or characteristic of the family Reduviidae
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Reduviidae, from Reduvius (genus name) + -idae (taxonomic suffix), from Latin reduvia (“a remainder, remnant, fragment”), describing the habit of the nymph of Reduvius personatus camouflaging itself with small pieces of debris.

parole.significato: One of several passerine birds in the genus Saltator.
parole.testo: Borrowed from the genus name, translingual Saltator, borrowed from Latin saltātor (“dancer”).

parole.significato: A plant in the genus Salvia, such as sage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Salvia, in turn from Latin salvia (“sage”). Doublet of sage.

parole.significato: A human being (Homo sapiens).
parole.testo: From translingual Homo sapiens, from Latin sapiēns, present active participle of sapiō (“discern, be capable of discerning”).

parole.significato: Cannabis sativa, a widely consumed form of cannabis.
parole.testo: Ellipsis of translingual Cannabis sativa (“sativa form of marijuana”), from Latin sativa (“cultivated”)

parole.significato: Any leguminous flowering plant of the genus Securigera, known vernacularly alongside members of the genus Coronilla (fr…
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Securigera, itself from Latin secūriger (“axebearing, axewielding”).

parole.significato: Any leguminous plant of the genus Senegalia, closely related to acacias, found across the Southern Hemisphere.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Senegalia, from Latin Senegalia (“Senegal”), equivalent to Senegal + -ia.

parole.significato: Any June beetle of the genus Serica.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Serica, from Latin sērica (“garments, silk”).

parole.significato: A nitrogenous base, CO.(NH.C₃H₅)₂, related to urea, and extracted from mustard oil
parole.testo: From translingual Sinapis + Latin oleum (“oil”) + -ine.

parole.significato: Any member of the Smilax genus of greenbriers; usually vines.
parole.testo: From the genus name, translingual Smilax. Further from Latin smīlax f and Ancient Greek σμῖλαξ f (smîlax).

parole.significato: Any plant in the genus Solanum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Translingual Solanum.

parole.significato: The goldenrod, or any of various similar plants in the genus Solidago.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Solidago, from Latin solidago.

parole.significato: Any of numerous species of grass in genus Spinifex, growing in sand dunes.
parole.testo: From translingual Spinifex (genus name), from Latin spina (“spine”) + Latin -fex (“maker”) (from Latin facere (“to make”)).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the family Sterculiaceae (a former name for Malvaceae) of polypetalous exogenous plants, mostly tropi…
parole.testo: From translingual Sterculia + -aceous, the typical genus, from Latin Sterculius (“the deity that presided over manuring”), from stercus (“dung”). So called because one of the original species has a foetid smell.

parole.significato: Any spinosaurid dinosaur in the genus Suchomimus from the Early Cretaceous Period.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Suchomimus, from sucho- + Latin mīmus (“mimic”).

parole.significato: Describing a member of an extinct order of corals, the Tabulata: having tabulae (well-developed horizontal internal par…
parole.testo: Back-formation from translingual Tabulata (“an extinct order of corals”) on the basis of -ate (adjective-forming suffix, corresponding to Latin -ātus (forming participles), itself seen in Tabulata), from Latin tabulāta, the nominative neuter plural of tabulātus (“floored”). See further at etymology

parole.significato: A termite.
parole.testo: From the translingual Termes (genus name), from Late Latin termes, late variant of Classical Latin tarmes (“woodworm”).

parole.significato: Any large tree and flowering plant of the genus Terminalia.
parole.testo: From translingual Terminalia + -an, from Latin terminus. From Proto-Indo-European *térmn̥ (“boundary”).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Trifolium of clovers and trefoils.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Trifolium, from Latin trifolium.

parole.significato: A marine gastropod of the family Turbinidae, or the shell thereof.
parole.testo: From a reanalysis or misconstruction of translingual Turbinidae (with the root Turbo), from a similar pronunciation. To demonstrate (in General American): Turbinidae as /tɝˈbɪ.nɪ.deɪ/ and turban as /ˈtɝ.bən/; as /ɪ/ and /ə/ are interchangeable in certain words in General American, especially before

parole.significato: Any flatworm of the class Turbellaria.
parole.testo: From translingual Turbellaria (from Latin turbellae (“bustle”), from turba (“confusion”)) + -an.

parole.significato: Any organism of the genus Ulva.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Ulva, itself from Latin ulva (“sedge”).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Vaccinium of ericaceous shrubs including the various kinds of blueberries and the true cranberries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Vaccinium, itself borrowed from Latin vaccīnium.

parole.significato: Any of the bivalve molluscs in the genus Venus or family Veneridae.
parole.testo: From translingual Venus (“a genus of clams”), from Latin.

parole.significato: A mullein (of genus Verbascum)
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Verbascum, from Latin verbascum.

parole.significato: Any of the many species of marine gastropods belonging to Vermetus and allied genera, of the family Vermetidae.
parole.testo: From translingual Vermetus, from Latin vermis (“worm”).

parole.significato: Any of a number of small insectivorous passerine birds, of the genus Vireo, that have grey-green plumage.
parole.testo: From translingual Vireo (genus name), from Latin vireō (“to be green”).

parole.significato: Any of several species of the genus Vitex.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Vitex, from Latin vītex.

parole.significato: Any protozoan of the genus Vorticella.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Vorticella, from Latin vortic- + -ella.

parole.significato: Streptocitta albicollis, a common species of myna often confused for a magpie due to its coloration, endemic to Indones…
parole.testo: white + necked + myna, a partial calque of translingual Streptocitta albicollis, from Latin albicollis (“white-necked”).

parole.significato: Synonym of swordfish.
parole.testo: Borrowed from translingual Xiphias or Latin xiphiās (“swordfish”).
